faq.a: Both parents may be carriers; each pregnancy has a 25 % chance the child inherits two mutant alleles.
faq.q: Why can a child be affected by an autosomal recessive disease if only one parent is a known carrier?

faq.a: Yes, if she is homozygous for the mutation or has skewed X‑inactivation causing manifest disease.

exam: A 12‑year‑old boy from a consanguineous marriage presents with severe anaemia and splenomegaly. Which inheritance pattern should you consider and why? — Autosomal recessive; both parents likely carriers, common for β‑thalassaemia in East Africa.

A female carrier of haemophilia A has a son with prolonged bleeding after circumcision. What is the most likely genotype of the son and the next step? — Hemizygous for the factor VIII mutation; give recombinant factor VIII and counsel family.

During a ward round you see a patient with joint pain, fever and a family history of sickle cell disease. What immediate investigation is appropriate if haemoglobin electrophoresis is unavailable? — Peripheral smear for sickled cells; start analgesia and hydration while arranging confirmatory testing.

A 30‑year‑old woman with a family history of Huntington disease asks about her risk. What information do you give? — 50 % chance of inheriting the mutant allele; discuss predictive testing and psychosocial support.

You suspect an X‑linked recessive disorder in a male patient with muscle weakness. Which clinical clue would help differentiate Duchenne from Becker muscular dystrophy? — Earlier onset (<5 years) and faster progression suggest Duchenne; both are X‑linked.

A newborn screening shows elevated phenylalanine. Which inheritance pattern does classic phenylketonuria follow and what is the first management step? — Autosomal recessive; start a low‑phenylalanine diet immediately.

In a resource‑limited hospital, a child with suspected thalassaemia major cannot get DNA analysis. Which simple test can support the diagnosis and what does it show? — CBC with high RBC count, low MCV and target cells; suggests thalassaemia.

A patient with known sickle cell disease presents with sudden chest pain and hypoxia. What life‑threatening complication must you rule out and how? — Acute chest syndrome; obtain chest X‑ray and start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, oxygen and transfusion.
ai.title: Genetic Inheritance Patterns
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Understanding how genes are passed helps clinicians recognise inherited disorders, counsel families and anticipate complications, especially where diagnostic resources are limited.

b: Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X‑linked, mitochondrial
Variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance modify presentation
sections.p: Genes are transmitted from parents to offspring in predictable ways. Recognising patterns guides diagnosis, risk assessment and counselling, even when molecular testing is unavailable.

b: Dominant allele masks recessive allele in heterozygotes
X‑linked genes reside on the X chromosome; males are hemizygous
sections.p: Each cell contains two copies of each autosomal gene (alleles). During meiosis, alleles segregate so each gamete receives one copy. The combination in the child determines phenotype.

b: Mosaicism can produce milder or segmental disease
sections.p: Gene expression is controlled by promoters, enhancers and epigenetic marks. Inherited mutations may affect coding sequence, splicing or regulatory regions, altering protein function.

b: Autosomal recessive: sickle cell disease, β‑thalassaemia
Autosomal dominant: Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome
X‑linked: haemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy
sections.p: Pathogenic variants disrupt normal protein activity, leading to disease. In low‑resource settings, common inherited disorders include sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, cystic fibrosis (rare), and hereditary deafness.

b: Sickle cell crisis → vaso‑occlusive pain, infection risk, acute chest syndrome
β‑thalassaemia major → severe anaemia, iron overload, cardiac failure
Haemophilia → spontaneous joint bleeds, intracranial haemorrhage
sections.p: Identifying inheritance patterns directs investigations, informs prognosis and guides family counselling. It also alerts clinicians to associated complications that may need urgent care.

t.b: What inheritance pattern is likely? – Reveals autosomal recessive vs dominant vs X‑linked
What does it show in sickle cell? – Sickled cells, target cells; supports diagnosis when haemoglobin electrophoresis unavailable
What does a low haemoglobin with high reticulocyte count indicate? – Hemolytic anaemia, prompting further genetic work‑up

b: Always ask about consanguinity for recessive disorders
Distinguish carrier state from disease in autosomal recessive families
Remember that X‑linked recessive diseases affect males more severely
sections.p: Examiners test ability to apply inheritance concepts to real patients, not just definitions.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute sickle cell crisis with chest pain or respiratory distress
Rapidly progressive neurological decline in a known genetic disorder
